thread.title: How Netflix's Oscar Obsession Could Impact Investors - Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX)

author: The Entertainment Oracle
title: How Netflix's Oscar Obsession Could Impact Investors - Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX)
text:
For the past few years, outside of Apple’s (NASDAQ: AAPL ) desire to enter the original TV space, the worst kept secret in the streaming space was that Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ) wants an Oscar.
Badly.
This isn’t a “we’ll get there” situation, this is an “I want it now” situation, and it doesn’t care who knows it. To Netflix, there’s nothing more important, and that’s been made very clear as of late with how it is handling the release of its latest big Oscar-bait film, Roma . The problem is, this obsession could also create a situation for investors that will have a long-term - but very real - negative impact.
Now, let’s be realistic, Roma would be a tough sell regardless of who distributed it, as it’s a black and white movie that isn’t in English. Adding the Netflix element just makes an already complicated situation even more complicated.
The point is that Netflix is bending over backwards to make Roma its House of Cards of the film world. To do that, though, it had to finally changing its stance on “windowing.” For those unfamiliar with the term, that refers to the window between when a film runs in theaters and when it can be made available for home viewing.
Traditionally, that is around a three-month period, and while Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) decided to play nice with exhibitors and honor that window, Netflix was steadfast about going day and date.
Guess what happened?
Amazon has scored multiple Oscar nominations (and wins) in top categories, and Netflix has barely been a blip on the radar. So now, in an effort to turn the tide, the streamer is back-tracking and allowing its films to have a small window between in-theater airing and streaming on the service.
Yep, a whole three weeks... for one film. And just seven days for two others.
Now, don’t get me wrong, Netflix relenting at all is a big deal, and this is a credit to film industry maverick Scott Stuber, who helped achieve this Herculean task. Stuber, a respected executive with a strong track record, was brought in by the service in 2017 to help sway favor towards the streamer.
The theory was spot on - bring in someone the industry likes in the hope they’ll be more open to conversations they don’t want to have. The problem is, these talks were always going to result in a compromise, and Stuber had the unenviable task of offering a solution that is the equivalent of saying “Two for me, one for you.”
The three-week window is a step in the right direction, whereas the one-week window is a joke and everyone knows it - including Academy members who are the ones voting (but more on that in a second).
The problem is, it also creates a situation that could get it into trouble with investors. While Roma is the film getting a three-week window, two other films are getting just one-week windows each, and that’s sending a message to its base that they are being prioritized.
Netflix’s allure has always been the mystery of how things are done, and one talent has no idea how the other is doing - it’s all what they are told by the company. Now, though, it is very clear what is “A” level and what is “B” level. If I were the Coen Brothers or Sandra Bullock, I’d be a little ticked that my film is getting a one-week run while Roma is getting a three-week run.
That potential level of internal competition is something Netflix has been able to avoid for years, but it could eventually bubble up. It could also cost the steamer where it hurts - getting new talent.
Netflix’s power in the industry is its ability to offer unlimited freedom and a seemingly unlimited budget to make somebody’s passion project. The downside, though, is nobody except for the company (and apparently its employees) has any idea how it ultimately does, so it’s hard to use it as benchmark for getting future projects greenlit.
There’s a great quote from an anonymous source in The Hollywood Reporter that pretty much hits the nail right on the head.
“They don't want to take the risk of having bad box office numbers. They are going to make assertions about how fantastic the crowds were, but there will be no dollars. There's no credibility because there's no accountability."
In fact, that’s the key reason why the author of Crazy Rich Asians opted against selling to the streamer despite a huge offer. He wanted the industry to see that a film fully starring Asian-American actors could be a success - and it was!
And those are areas investors need to pay attention. I used the analogy earlier about how Netflix wants Roma to be its House of Cards , but it is also fitting here to make sure investors realize Netflix in many ways is a “house of cards” in and of itself - albeit a very steady one (for now).
However, things like this cause more of a sway to the house, as it adds a new wrinkle. The “con” category to a Netflix deal really only had that one point about number/viewer transparency - now comes a second: Will my film get a Roma push? It’s a dangerous precedent the company is setting - and one that will follow it.
Will that added question change the value proposition for filmmakers?
And then, there’s this.
Right now, there is a very real battle going on both inside the Academy of Motion Picture Arts & Sciences and internationally about the Netflix problem. Just like the television world, studios changed the rules to allows streamers into the awards mix - and now, it’s coming back to bite them.
On one hand, you have its supporters and showcasing how this helps the world of cinema in general, and on the other, you have the old-school traditionalists who still carry sway (i.e., Steven Spielberg and Christopher Nolan).
You are also now seeing overseas legislation coming to pass that will mandate movies open in theaters first before streaming. The idea there is to use the government to help protect cinemas and, in turn, the traditional method.
However, you also have ones in the middle who recognize Netflix is changing its stripes, but also that it may not be enough.
That alone is a big factor that could sway filmmakers from selling to Netflix, and that’s a potentially big hit for investors, as Netflix has now transitioned from needing IP, to creating its own IP - but it still needs the right talent giving the company that new IP. There is also no turning back, as studios and networks have wised up about the beast they have created and won’t make the mistake again.
Yes, Netflix stock is high and has been high, and aside from a bump or two in earnings every few cycles, it’s been solid - but it wouldn’t be the first to slide from the top after a misfire or two.
The most important thing here, though, is I’m not saying Netflix is done and I’m not saying you need to sell your stock. I’m saying just be aware the company is about to double down in a way that could have a dangerous long-term impact.
I stand by my belief that Oscars and Emmys do play a big role in the health of a company and both bring extraordinary value, even if that doesn’t result in a financial bump - but there comes a point.
And Netflix is getting perilously close.
Regardless of whether Roma succeeds or fails, Netflix is going to have to answer for its approach - to its board, to its partners, to its future talent and, most importantly, to its investors. While it would be nice to have the little gold guy in hand when it does, it may also not make a difference.
